theory.intro: A sample is chosen from a population. How the members are chosen, and how many answer, affect how well the result represents the population. A large sample does not put right an unfair choice of members.
facts: **Selection bias** — the selected group does not accurately represent the population. Surveying only basketball players about students’ heights may give a misleading result.
**Small sample size** — a very small sample may miss the variety of views or experiences in the population.
**Volunteer bias** — people choose whether to participate. Those who reply may have different views from those who do not reply.
**Survivorship bias** — the sample includes successful cases but leaves out failures.
More replies to an open survey do not remove volunteer bias. Check who could reply and who actually replied, not just the number of replies.
steps: Identify the population the investigation is about
Identify who is included in the sample and who is left out
Explain how their views or experiences may differ
Check whether the sample is too small to represent the population’s variety

workedExamples.question_text:
A council wants to find the mean income of all residents in a city. It surveys $90$ residents who live in wealthy waterfront neighbourhoods.
Explain why the sample may be unrepresentative.
workedExamples.solution_text:
The population is all residents in the city.
The sample includes only residents of wealthy waterfront neighbourhoods and leaves out residents elsewhere.
These residents may have higher incomes than other residents, so the sample may overestimate the city’s mean income.
**This is selection bias**.

workedExamples.question_text:
A school wants to know the percentage of its $840$ students who have maths as their favourite subject. It surveys only the $28$ students in its Year 12 Maths Extension class.
Describe the sampling bias.
workedExamples.solution_text:
The population is all $840$ students at the school.
Only students in the Year 12 Maths Extension class are included.
These students may be more interested in maths than students in other classes and year levels.
The sample may overestimate the percentage who have maths as their favourite subject.
**This is selection bias**.

workedExamples.question_text:
A council wants to know farmers’ opinions about a new road. It asks $3$ farmers from a community of $640$.
Explain why this sample may be unrepresentative.
workedExamples.solution_text:
The population is all $640$ farmers in the community.
Only $3$ farmers are surveyed.
Their opinions may differ from those of the other $637$ farmers, and the sample may miss much of the variety of opinions.
**The sample size is too small to give a reliable picture of the community’s views**.

workedExamples.question_text:
Researchers invite adults in a town to volunteer for a study about eating habits. Only $75$ health-conscious adults volunteer.
Explain why the sample may be unrepresentative.
workedExamples.solution_text:
The population is all adults in the town.
The sample includes only the health-conscious adults who volunteered.
Their eating habits may differ from those of adults who did not volunteer.
**This is volunteer bias**.

foundation.question_text:
Marlow Museum emails all $4200$ of its members a link to a survey about its exhibitions, and reports the answers of the $310$ members who chose to reply.
Explain why the sample may be unrepresentative.
foundation.solution_text:
The population is all $4200$ museum members.
Only the $310$ members who chose to reply are included.
$4200-310=3890$ members did not reply.
Their views may differ from those of the members who replied, for example because members with strong opinions may be more likely to answer.
**The sample may be unrepresentative because of volunteer bias**.

foundation.question_text:
An insurance company asks $5$ of its $20\,000$ policyholders how they rate its claims service, and reports the result as the view of its policyholders.
Explain why this result is unreliable.
foundation.solution_text:
With only $5$ responses, one unusually happy or unusually angry policyholder changes the reported figure by a fifth.
Five people may miss much of the range of experiences across $20\,000$ policyholders.
**The sample is far too small for the result to be relied on**.

foundation.question_text:
A bus depot wants to know how its $160$ drivers rate the new rosters. It puts up a notice asking for volunteers and surveys the $24$ drivers who volunteer.
Explain why this sample may be unrepresentative.
foundation.solution_text:
The population is all $160$ drivers at the depot.
Only the $24$ volunteers are included.
$160-24=136$ drivers are left out.
Drivers with strong opinions about the rosters may be more likely to volunteer, so their views may differ from those of other drivers.
**This is volunteer bias**.

development.question_text:
A bank shows a pop-up in its app asking customers to rate its service. Of its $350\,000$ customers, $10\,000$ choose to reply.
Explain why the result may not represent all its customers, despite the large number of replies.
development.solution_text:
The population is all $350\,000$ bank customers.
Only customers who use the app, see the pop-up and choose to reply are included.
$350\,000-10\,000=340\,000$ customers do not reply.
Customers who do not use the app are excluded, and those who volunteer to answer may have different views from other customers.
**The sample risks selection bias and volunteer bias**.
A large number of replies does not supply the missing customers’ views.

development.question_text:
The Riverton Swim Club wants to know how its $450$ members rate the new pool timetable. It posts a survey on the club’s social-media page and uses the replies to represent all members.
Explain why the sample may be unrepresentative.
development.solution_text:
The population is all $450$ club members.
Members who do not use the social-media page or do not see the survey are left out.
Of those who see it, only members who choose to reply are included. Members with strong views may be more likely to answer.
**The sample risks selection bias and volunteer bias**, because the respondents may have different views from other members.

development.question_text:
A hardware chain surveys $6$ of its $900$ employees, chosen at random, and reports that its staff are satisfied with the new rosters.
Explain the weakness in this study.
development.solution_text:
Random selection does not remove the weakness of surveying only $6$ employees.
$900-6=894$ employees are not surveyed.
One employee accounts for $\frac{1}{6}$ of the responses, so a few unusual experiences can have a large effect on the result.
The sample may miss much of the variety of views across the workforce.
**The sample size is too small to give a reliable picture of all employees’ views**.

mastery.question_text:
An airline emailed a satisfaction survey to all $800\,000$ passengers who flew with it last year, and $18\,000$ chose to reply.
Its report says the result reliably represents all its passengers because $18\,000$ is a very large sample.
Explain why this conclusion may not be valid.
mastery.solution_text:
The population is all $800\,000$ passengers who flew with the airline last year.
Only the $18\,000$ passengers who chose to reply are included.
$800\,000-18\,000=782\,000$ passengers did not reply.
Passengers with particularly good or bad experiences may be more likely to respond, so their satisfaction may differ from that of non-respondents.
**The conclusion may not be valid because of volunteer bias**.
Having many replies does not show that the sample represents the passengers who did not reply.

mastery.question_text:
A supermarket chain wants to know how all its $3600$ staff rate the new rosters. It surveys only its $180$ store managers and uses their answers to represent all staff.
Explain why this sample may give a distorted picture of all staff members’ views.
mastery.solution_text:
The population is all $3600$ staff members.
The sample includes only the $180$ store managers.
$3600-180=3420$ other staff members are left out.
Managers’ responsibilities and experiences of the rosters may differ from those of other staff, so their views may also differ.
**This is selection bias: a sample containing only managers may not represent all staff**.
